text.p: By Jim Middleton (ABC TV political correspondent)
Welcome home John Howard, welcome home to the chilly scenes of winter.

The prime minister had one genuine success during his two weeks abroad -- influencing President Clinton to stand by his opposition to prescribed, uniform greenhouse gas reduction targets despite pressure from his own deputy, Vice President Al Gore.

Even that was marred, though, by the prime minister's decision not to put his money where his mouth was in the international spotlight, the Earth Summit in New York. Even though he was only four hours down the road in Washington at the time.
The prime minister did return to strengthened retail sales figures -- adding weight to the government's argument that the patchy economy is gaining speed.
And there was a dividend from Moody's too -- its signal that, given fiscal good behaviour, Australia can expect its credit rating to be upgraded in the nearish future.
There, though, the good news stops. The rest is all hard slog, some of it very problematic indeed. As it is for the Opposition.

Labor may have Small Business Minister Geoff Prosser on the ropes. The ALP may also have reached the middle of this political cycle in better shape than it expected immediately after the 1996 election cycle, but there are worrying signs for Kim Beazley too.
Younger frontbenchers, notably Lindsay Tanner and Mark Latham, are barely toeing the line.
Simon Crean's leadership ambition is palpable, Gareth Evans is still visibly uncomfortable more than a year after his transition to opposition and the House of Representatives.

The government may be losing way in the polls, but senior Labor strategists -- looking at the published polls -- privately point out the coalition has a comfortable base of support from which to strike out for a second term.

Things may have gone worse for the government far more quickly than Labor could have dreamed last Christmans, but the hardheads still believe everything will have to go wrong for the government and everything right for the ALP to give the Opposition any chance of success at the next election.

Some of the keenest psephologists in the Labor party have even done a seat-by-seat analysis, factoring in the strengths and weaknesses of coalition and ALP candidates. Their hardboiled assessment -- Labor simply cannot do it from here.

Kim Beazley is setting great store by his "Back to the Future" approach, drawing comfort from the success of the Opposition's car tariff backflip. Not only did it pressure the government to follow suit, but it's almost the only issue which has given Labor any defining profile with the voters. So heartened was the ALP by the impact of its car tariff switch that it also did the same on the sugar tariff -- and with even less reason.

The opposition's head in the sand approach to tax reform is not likely to help Labor's cause either. Beazley and those around him are convinced the coalition's so far ill-defined and somewhat undisciplined approach to the subject guarantees that the government will be as vulnerable to a scare campaign as was John Hewson and Fightback! in 1993. However, it may not be as simple as that.
Peter Costello, in particular, is starting out on a more modest and more sophisticated tax journey.
Already, he's managed to keep the welfare lobby in the cart, which is more than Hewson ever managed.
To have ACOSS describe an encounter with the coalition on tax as "excellent" is a coup indeed.
In addition, all the telltale signs from the treasurer point to a much more realistic tax reform programme than Fightback!

It seems that Costello is determined any broadening of the indirect tax base must produce a goods and services tax levied at no more than 10 percent. Apart from reducing the possibility of frightening the horses, it insulates the federal government from special pleading.
For instance, it means the states' demand for an end to payroll tax can be more easily resisted.
The treasurer has also signalled his readiness to consider reform on the income tax front -- trusts and the like.
Indeed, that's ACOSS' key pre-condition for staying in the cart and has the advantage of extending the coalition's "tough but fair" image.
In addition, by levying a GST at a modest level -- simply replacing the revenue currently gained by the WST -- produces another potential benefit.
The government could consider having a package which is revenue negative in the first year, but, because the take would grow with consumption, would turn revenue positive quite rapidly.
That might be harder for Labor to counter than was Fightback!
Welcome home John Howard.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
